source_text:
Nimis contristatus sum pro Valente, qui presbyter factus est aliquando apud vos, quod sic ignoret is locum qui datus est ei. Moneo itaque ut abstineatis vos ab avaritia et sitis casti veraces. Abstinete vos ab omni malo.
Qui autem non potest se in his gubernare, quomodo alii pronuntiat hoc? Si quis non se abstinuerit ab avaritia, ab idololatria coinquinabitur et tamquam inter gentes iudicabitur, qui ignorant iudicium domini. Aut nescimus, quia sancti mundum iudicabunt? sicut Paulus docet.
Ego autem nihil tale sensi in vobis vel audivi, in quibus laboravit beatus Paulus, qui estis in principio epistulae eius. De vobis etenim gloriatur in omnibus ecclesiis, quae dominum solae tunc cognoverant; nos autem nondum cognoveramus.
Valde ergo, fratres, contristor pro illo et pro coniuge eius, quibus det dominus paenitentiam veram. Sobrii ergo estote et vos in hoc; et non sicut inimicos tales existimetis, sed sicut passibilia membra et errantia eos revocate, ut omnium vestrum corpus salvetis. Hoc enim agentes vos ipsos aedificatis.
thought_title: Grief over Valens and a call to restore the fallen gently
orientation: Polycarp, writing with his fellow elders, turns from general exhortation to the specific case of Valens, a former elder among the Philippians who fell into love of money.
pass_a_gloss: I have been exceedingly grieved for Valens, who was made an elder once among you, because he is so ignorant of the place that was given to him. I warn therefore that you keep yourselves from love of money and be pure and truthful. Keep yourselves from all evil. But he who cannot govern himself in these things, how does he proclaim this to another? If anyone has not kept himself from love of money, he will be defiled by idolatry and will be judged as among the gentiles, who are ignorant of the judgment of the Lord. Or do we not know that the holy ones will judge the world? as Paul teaches. But I have perceived nothing of such a kind in you or heard, in whom the blessed Paul labored, who are in the beginning of his letter. For he boasts about you in all the churches, which alone had known the Lord at that time; but we had not yet known him. Greatly therefore, brothers, I am grieved for him and for his wife, to whom may the Lord give true repentance. Be sober-minded therefore, you also, in this matter; and do not consider such people as enemies, but call them back as suffering and straying members, so that you may save the body of all of you. For in doing this you build up yourselves.

choices.why: The glossary fixes this rendering for φιλαργυρία, the vice Polycarp warns against; the Latin avaritia stands for that Greek term.
The glossary fixes 'elders' for πρεσβύτεροι, the church office Valens once held.
Keeps the bodily metaphor and the two participles distinct: they are members of the body who suffer and have gone astray, not enemies.

choices.english: to whom may the Lord give true repentance
choices.why: Preserves the optative force of the subjunctive as a prayer-wish for Valens and his wife.
rejected: whom the Lord gives true repentance
to whom the Lord should give true repentance

choices.english: in the beginning of his letter
choices.why: Renders the Latin literally; Paul's letter to the Philippians opens by addressing the saints there, which is the point of the allusion.
rejected: at the start of his epistle
in the opening of his letter

bible_refs.note: quia sancti mundum iudicabunt (the holy ones will judge the world), introduced by 'as Paul teaches'

pass_b_english: I am deeply grieved for Valens, who was once made an elder among you, because he has so little understanding of the place that was given to him. I urge you, therefore, to keep yourselves from the love of money and to be pure and truthful. Keep yourselves from every evil.

If someone cannot govern himself in these matters, how can he proclaim them to another? If anyone does not keep himself from the love of money, he will be defiled by idolatry and will be judged as though among the gentiles, who do not know the judgment of the Lord. Or do we not know that the holy ones will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2)? As Paul teaches.

I have neither perceived nor heard of any such thing among you, among whom the blessed Paul labored and who are in the beginning of his letter. For he boasts about you in all the churches, which alone knew the Lord at that time; we had not yet known him.

So then, brothers and sisters, I am greatly grieved for him and for his wife, and may the Lord give them true repentance. Be sober-minded, then, in this matter yourselves as well. Do not regard such people as enemies, but call them back as suffering and straying members, so that you may save the body of all of you. For in doing this you build up yourselves.

last_rejected.why: The brief marks Paul as quoted teaching introduced by 'as Paul teaches' in Latin portion. English matches. Correct.
last_rejected.ruling: Reporter confirms 'As Paul teaches' correctly renders 'sicut Paulus docet'. No error.

last_rejected.why: 'Passibilia' means capable of suffering/susceptible to suffering, not 'suffering' as active participle. 'Suffering members' misrepresents the sense; these are frail, fallible members, not ones currently undergoing suffering.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Passibilia' as 'suffering' is within normal range; 'passibilia membra' = members capable of suffering, rendered adequately.

last_rejected.quote: the body of all of you
last_rejected.why: 'Omnium vestrum' is genitive plural, 'of all of you'. 'The body of all of you' captures this. But 'corpus' here means the body as whole community, 'your whole body'. The English is slightly awkward but not wrong.
last_rejected.ruling: Reporter admits 'body of all of you' captures 'omnium vestrum corpus' and is 'not wrong.' No error.

last_rejected.quote: who alone knew the Lord at that time; we had not yet known him
last_rejected.source_quote: quae dominum solae tunc cognoverant; nos autem nondum cognoveramus
last_rejected.why: English omits 'solae' (alone/only). The churches 'alone' knew the Lord—this exclusivity is lost, weakening Paul's boast and the historical point about Philippian priority.
last_rejected.fix: which alone knew the Lord at that time; we had not yet known him
last_rejected.ruling: 'Which alone knew' renders 'quae...solae...cognoverant.' 'Alone' is present in English. No omission.

last_rejected.why: 'Sic ignoret' means 'he is so ignorant of'/'he disregards thus', not 'has so little understanding'. 'Ignoret' is stronger—he ignores/disregards, not merely lacks understanding. This softens Valens's fault.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Ignoret' covers both 'be ignorant of' and 'disregard.' 'So little understanding' is within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: the place that was given to him
last_rejected.why: 'Locus' here means office/position, not physical place. 'Place' is ambiguous in English; 'position' or 'office' clearer for the ecclesiastical context.
last_rejected.fix: the office that was given to him
last_rejected.ruling: 'Place' can mean 'position/office' in English. Within normal range; mere preference for 'position' is not a major error.
